Supplier Slip-Ups: How Malpractices Can Bite into Restaurant Market Value Highlights  Supplier issues have a negative effect on restaurant market value.  Indirect linkage to a supplier issue has a decreased effect.  Different issues lead to varying effects on a restaurant’s market value. Abstract Ethical, environmental, and human rights standards are critical issues in the tourism and hospitality industry. In this context, restaurants must choose third-party members—such as suppliers—that align with their quality and sustainability standards, especially because these third-party members may encounter challenges related to food safety, ethical misconduct, environmental matters, and human rights violations. This study analyzes whether the market holds restaurants accountable for the shortcomings of their suppliers, even when the restaurant has not directly participated in or caused these problems. Based on signaling theory and the associative network memory paradigm, this study finds that supplier issues negatively affect the market value of restaurants, with indirect linkage exerting a greater impact than direct linkage, which informs these theories by underscoring the importance of memory and associations dynamics. Keywords: supplier issues; restaurant market value; signaling theory; hospitality industry. 1 INTRODUCTION Culinary experiences, where restaurants play a fundamental role, have evolved beyond mere sustenance and have become a pivotal aspect of the overall travel experience (Kivela and Crotts, 2006, 2009; Stone et al., 2022; Vrontis et al., 2022; Miocevic and Mikulic, 2023). However, the restaurant industry is currently undergoing substantial changes in supply chain management due to strong competition and pressure for socially and environmentally responsible practices. Prioritizing economic value alone is deemed insufficient (Hassini, Surti, and Searcy, 2012), and in response, restaurants have been revising their supplier selection to incorporate new criteria, including environmental sustainability, social responsibility, and customer satisfaction (Taherdoost and Bard, 2019). This strategic shift enables them to uphold high-quality standards, meet customer expectations, and align with evolving social norms (Chen et al., 2021). The principle of “buying right to sell right” has always been fundamental in the food service industry (Reynolds, 1966). When purchasing products, restaurants must consider not only the quality of raw materials but also the standards of their suppliers. Responsible purchasing involves continuous monitoring to ensure that suppliers adhere to ethical, sustainable, and environmentally friendly practices that align with the restaurant’s values (Marshall et al., 2015). Numerous studies have extensively examined the positive effects of implementing social and food safety practices on the individual performances of hospitality companies or suppliers (Shin et al., 2021; Nicolau, 2008; Mathe, 2012; Pullman, Maloni, and Carter, 2009). Also, studies have also explored the negative impact on performance resulting from the failure to adhere to these practices (Kang, Lee, and Huh, 2010; Seo, Jang, Miao, Almanza, and Behnke, 2013; Kabir, Watson, and Somaratna, 2018). However, the literature has not yet explored how non-compliance with these practices on the one side may influence the reputation and performance of the other side. 2 Therefore, our research question is: how do suppliers’ malpractices affect restaurants’ market value? The restaurant industry faces distinct challenges in supplier relationships and operational demands that set it apart from other sectors. Restaurants operate in highly visible environments where supplier quality has a direct and immediate impact on the dining experience, with any supplier issues becoming apparent to customers quickly (Mhlanga, 2024). For example, a supplier's failure to meet sustainability standards can tarnish a restaurant's reputation, especially given the industry's reliance on fresh, high-quality ingredients and growing consumer demand for transparency in sourcing. Additionally, the restaurant industry is subject to unique pressures, such as stringent health and safety regulations and the need for fast supply turnarounds (Diaz, 2024). These operational demands increase the risk for restaurants when supplier reliability falters, as this can directly impact customer satisfaction and business performance. In contrast, other sectors may experience more diffuse consequences from similar disruptions (Bordian et al., 2024). While Kim et al. (2019) include restaurants in a broader category of “Wholesale & retail trade,” their analysis fails to fully capture these industry-specific challenges. Our study aims to fill this gap by focusing solely on the restaurant industry, offering a more in-depth analysis of the unique supplier-related pressures it faces. Additionally, recent trends and developments within the restaurant industry make this study particularly timely. The landscape of the restaurant industry is continually evolving, influenced by changing consumer preferences, technological advancements, and societal shifts. In recent years, there has been a noticeable surge in consumer awareness and demand for sustainable and socially responsible practices within the foodservice sector. This increased consciousness extends beyond just the food served and encompasses the entire supply chain, including the sourcing practices of 3 restaurant suppliers. With consumers increasingly prioritizing ethical considerations in their purchasing decisions (Fakfare et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Picasso et ell., 2023; Yang and Kirillova, 2023), restaurant operators are under mounting pressure to ensure that their suppliers adhere to stringent sustainability and ethical standards. Technological advancements, such as online review platforms and social media, empower consumers to hold businesses accountable, making lapses in supplier compliance potential public relations crises for restaurants. While Seo et al. (2013) explore supplier-restaurant relationships, they focus on safety issues, neglecting concerns like sustainability and social responsibility. Addressing these gaps, our study aims to provide timely insights for stakeholders. Building trust between restaurants and their stakeholders relies on this commitment. Although restaurants control internal procedures, they cannot directly influence supplier behavior, which can lead to challenges such as food safety, ethical issues, environmental concerns, and human rights violations. To address this gap in the literature, this study aims to investigate the effects of supplier issues on the market values of restaurants that choose to collaborate with them. Building on the conceptual framework of signaling theory (Spence, 1973), the central question is whether restaurants are held accountable by the market for the missteps of their suppliers, even in cases where the restaurants are not directly involved in these issues. Additionally, this study seeks to investigate whether different types of supplier-related problems lead to distinct repercussions for these restaurants. Furthermore, supplier issues are categorized into two types based on how the market becomes aware of them through news, each potentially having a different impact on the restaurant: direct and indirect links. In the case of direct links, news articles often mention the names of the restaurants dealing with the troubled supplier to attract more readers, directly associating the supplier’s issue with the restaurants. By contrast, indirect links occur when news articles do not 4 disclose the names of the restaurants working with the troubled supplier. With indirect links, linking the supplier’s issues to restaurants is more challenging for the market. To explain this indirect link, we refer to Collins and Loftus’s (1975) associative network memory paradigm. This study focuses on both the direct and indirect links to comprehensively understand their respective impacts on restaurant market value. EFFECTS OF A SUPPLIER’S MALPRACTICES ON RESTAURANT MARKET VALUE In the hospitality industry, the relationship between retailers and suppliers is symbiotic, with both parties relying on each other to achieve their goals (Murphy and Smith, 2009). Retailers depend on suppliers for essential products and services, while suppliers count on retailers to purchase and promote their offerings. Efficient collaboration with these external entities is crucial for a restaurant’s success (Aigbedo, 2021). Intense competition in the hospitality sector has led companies to depend heavily on key suppliers (Salihoğlu and Gezici, 2018), making the effective selection of suppliers a critical asset. Suppliers’ expertise in areas such as product and service quality, cost, and delivery greatly affects the purchasing companies’ ability to provide defect-free products to their clients (Wang et al., 2024). The growing pressure from consumers, grassroots organizations, community groups, government entities, shareholders, and competitors for socially and environmentally responsible business practices has necessitated a broader approach to supplier selection (Hassini et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2024). As a result, considerations of environmental, social, political, and customer satisfaction factors have become integral to the process (Taherdoost and Bard, 2019). 5 While the emphasis on broader corporate responsibility criteria has increased (Wu et al., 2024), it is important to recognize that supplier agreements and contracts have historically included provisions related to food safety and environmental responsibilities (Starbird, 2005). Many suppliers are required to adhere to voluntary standards such as Good Agricultural Practices or regulatory requirements (Priya and Singh, 2024), ensuring that certain operational standards are met. These measures have been a part of supply chain management to some degree and continue to evolve in their rigor and enforcement. Publicly traded restaurants demonstrate their commitment to these criteria by incorporating them into their annual reports, which they file with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). For instance, Chipotle Mexican Grill, in their 2023 SEC annual report, stated, “we strive to serve only meats that are raised in accordance with criteria we have established in an effort to improve sustainability and promote animal welfare … by which we mean produce grown by suppliers whose practices conform to our Food With Integrity standards and our priorities with respect to environmental considerations and employee welfare … suppliers we carefully select based on quality, price, availability, and the suppliers’ understanding of and adherence to our mission and Food With Integrity standards.” Therefore, selecting capable suppliers who meet most, if not all, of these criteria is an essential part of ensuring the quality, safety, and value of products and services for restaurants and their customers (Huang, 2023). Doing so can increase customer satisfaction, reduce operational costs, improve the restaurant’s financial position, and boost the restaurant’s reputation (Zhong, Ma, Tu, and Li, 2016). Restaurants typically strive to choose the best suppliers to fulfill their needs and uphold social, environmental, and quality standards (Martínez-López and Vargas-Sánchez, 2013), openly 6 disclosing the review methods used to consistently ensure adherence to these standards. Nonetheless, these suppliers may encounter various internal challenges that contradict these established standards. Noteworthy examples include food safety issues; ethical/malpractice issues such as corruption, bribery, food fraud, discrimination, and animal welfare; environmental issues; and human rights issues. Several major food and beverage suppliers have faced controversies related to the aforementioned issues. In 2011, Tyson Foods, a supplier for McDonald’s, resolved a bribery case with the SEC over allegations that its Mexican subsidiary had made improper payments to government veterinarians to expedite the approval of its products. In 2014, a Chinese meat supplier providing goods to Starbucks was found selling expired meat. The central question raised is whether restaurants face market scrutiny for malpractices committed by their suppliers, even when the restaurant is not directly involved in these matters. To address this inquiry, we must understand how adverse reports regarding a supplier’s malpractice or issue may be linked to the restaurant itself. Supplier issues as bad signals for restaurants Signaling theory, a robust conceptual framework gaining prominence in management research (Bergh, Connelly, Ketchen, and Shannon, 2014) and explanations for investment decision-making (Alsos and Ljunggren, 2017), plays a pivotal role in focusing on the management’s objective of conveying information and obtaining feedback from the market, stakeholders, and the broader community. Information asymmetries can bring about conflicts within an organizational context, but signaling helps alleviate this by transmitting pertinent and high-quality information to various parties (Connelly et al., 2011; Taj, 2016). 7 Comprising four components—the signaler, signals, receiver, and feedback—signaling theory aligns with the fundamental communication channel (Connelly et al., 2011; Taj, 2016). In a business context, management insiders typically act as signalers when disseminating positive signals, such as the strategic selection of suppliers that align with the restaurant’s values of quality and sustainability. However, when negative issues arise from suppliers, such as food safety concerns or ethical breaches, the suppliers themselves may inadvertently act as the initial signalers if these issues become public. Nonetheless, the restaurant must also manage these signals, deciding how to respond and thus potentially becoming a co-signaler by either addressing the issues transparently or failing to act, which itself sends a significant signal to the market. The flow of information serves as signals, and the receivers, outsiders without access to insider information, rely on these signals to form perceptions. Feedback represents the interplay between signalers and receivers (Connelly et al., 2011; Morris, 1987; Mavlanova et al., 2012; Taj, 2016). In the signaling procedure, the key participants are the signaler and the receiver, and the signals transmit either favorable or unfavorable information to rectify information asymmetries. Favorable signals enhance company value and performance, whereas unfavorable signals diminish stock prices and product demand (Morris, 1987; Dionne and Ouederni, 2011). In the context of restaurants (signalers), their choices and actions, such as selecting suppliers, communicate information about product quality and social commitment. These signals reach receivers— customers, investors, and the public—who lack direct supplier information. When supplier problems arise, negative signals can harm a restaurant’s market value. Effectively communicating efforts to address these issues, such as improving quality control or selecting more responsible suppliers, allows restaurants to send positive signals that counteract the negative impact. The 8 signaling process influences how consumers, investors, and the market perceive a restaurant’s ability to handle supplier-related challenges. Lucking-Reiley et al. (2007) note that consumers tend to assign varying importance to positive and negative information, a phenomenon known as negativity bias. Negative information carries more weight than positive information, as elucidated by Klein (1996) and Skowronski and Carlston (1989). Scholars argue that negative information generally has a more substantial impact than positive information (Richey et al., 1975). Research by Maheswaran and Meyers-Levy (1990) and Skowronski and Carlston (1989) suggests that negative information holds greater informativeness and diagnostic value in the consumer decision-making process. Ba and Pavlou (2002) and Chevalier and Mayzlin (2006) demonstrate that negative information has a more significant impact on a company’s financial situation and price premiums than positive information. This aligns with the notion of consumer decision- making involving perceived risk between alternatives, a concept central to the prospect theory developed by Kahneman and Tversky (1979). People tend to base their choices on the potential for losses rather than prospective gains in accordance with this theory. This phenomenon elevates the importance of negative information in decision-making processes. In our context, news items primarily originate from the media rather than the companies themselves. In such a situation, apart from social media (Rathjens et al., 2024), the traditional media can play a crucial role in disseminating information and assisting external investors in making decisions, as indicated by Lee and Wang (2017). Guldiken et al. (2017) observed that numerous studies employing signaling theory reveal signals do not always need to originate directly from the sender. For example, prior research shows that the media often provide signals regarding companies (e.g., Daniel and Titman, 2006; Deephouse, 2000). 9 Note that media coverage can transform supplier issues into signals. When a restaurant’s suppliers face negative issues related to food quality, ethical practices, environmental concerns, or human rights violations, these issues act as signals to the restaurant’s stakeholders (Li, Chen, Liang, and Yang, 2022). This transformation of supplier issues into signals through media coverage is pivotal as it increases the visibility and perceived seriousness of these issues, shaping stakeholder perceptions. Stakeholders often attribute the actions or misdeeds of a supplier to the restaurants themselves due to the restaurants’ responsibility for their supply chain, reflecting on their overall commitment to corporate responsibility. Consequently, stakeholders may interpret the negative supplier signals as indicative of the restaurant’s lack of commitment to quality, ethical standards, environmental responsibility, or human rights, and this perception can affect their trust in the company and their willingness to engage with it (Konuk, 2023). Furthermore, in a highly competitive market, customers aware of such issues might switch to competitors not merely out of safety concerns but also driven by ethical considerations, seeking brands whose values align more closely with their own. Moreover, customers may choose to purchase products or services from competitors who have better supplier practices, leading to decreased sales and potential damage to the company’s brand image (Lee and Jin, 2019). Similarly, investors, attuned to the potential for reputational damage and subsequent loss of customer loyalty, may perceive the company as a riskier investment. The possibility of future scandals or regulatory penalties that could arise from poor supplier practices further compounds this risk, leading to reduced investment and potentially negatively impacting the company’s stock price (Zhang et al., 2024). Therefore, in accordance with signaling theory and recognizing the negative effect of unfavorable signals on a company’s performance, we propose the following hypothesis: H1: Bad news regarding a supplier negatively impact restaurants’ market value. 10 Indirect versus direct links Supplier issues can be divided into two categories based on how they come to the market’s attention, each exerting a distinct impact on restaurants: indirect connections and direct connections. Indirect connections arise when news articles refrain from mentioning the names of restaurants associated with the troubled supplier, presenting a greater challenge for the market to link the supplier’s problems to the restaurant. In contrast, direct connections occur when news articles explicitly identify the restaurants involved with the affected supplier, often with the aim of attracting a larger readership. This results in a direct association between the supplier’s problem and the restaurant. Indirect link Cues related to business transparency, encompassing information transparency and exposure, play a major role in influencing the perceptions of customers and their decisions (Springer and Whittaker, 2018), reinforcing the association within the supply chain. Transparency is particularly crucial in the hospitality industry for building brand loyalty and trust among external stakeholders who may lack detailed background information (Busser and Shulga, 2019; Tapscott and Ticoll, 2003). Martínez and Crowther (2008) emphasize transparency as a method for shifting power from the company to its stakeholders, thereby minimizing information asymmetry and allowing for well-informed assessments of the company’s products. Although companies traditionally safeguard supply chain information for competitive advantage, voluntary disclosure can enhance sales, build public trust, and generate word-of-mouth marketing (Pettey, 2018). However, rising consumer demands for transparency in food production, ingredients, and supply chains have led to its integration into contemporary food supply chains. This transparency allows stakeholders 11 access to accurate, pertinent, and timely information regarding products within the supply chain (Wognum et al., 2011). In transparent supply chains, information is easily accessible, swift, and comprehensible (Trienekens et al., 2012), fortifying the association between a restaurant and its supplier. Collins and Loftus’ (1975) associative network memory paradigm offers a suitable theoretical framework to elucidate how restaurant stakeholders may link suppliers’ problems to the restaurant’s reputation. According to this paradigm, memory comprises a network of concepts (nodes) linked through associations. When stakeholders encounter information about a supplier’s problem, even if the restaurant is not explicitly mentioned in media, these stakeholders may activate interconnected concepts in the memory network, such as the restaurant’s name. This activation can lead to the creation of new associations between the supplier’s problem and the restaurant’s image (Jung and Lee, 2022). The extensive media coverage and public discussions, even when not directly naming the restaurant, can reinforce these associations due to the existing relationship between the restaurant and its suppliers. Overall, Collins and Loftus’ paradigm suggests that restaurant stakeholders may indirectly link suppliers’ malpractices to the restaurant’s image through the activation and creation of associations in their memory network. In practical terms, this connection can occur through several mechanisms. First, consumers, investors, or other stakeholders who are familiar with the restaurant’s suppliers through prior publicity, such as news reports, public supplier agreements, or even marketing campaigns, may already have formed associations between the restaurant and its suppliers. For example, if a restaurant has publicly emphasized its relationship with a specific supplier due to ethical sourcing or sustainability claims, this information becomes part of the stakeholders' mental framework. 12 Thus, even when the restaurant is not mentioned in the article about the supplier's problem, stakeholders may recall this prior association, linking the issue back to the restaurant. Furthermore, industry knowledge plays a crucial role in forming these connections. Stakeholders with a deeper understanding of supply chain structures, such as investors, industry analysts, or even well-informed consumers, might recognize that certain suppliers service specific types of restaurants. This familiarity with the industry can lead them to infer potential relationships between the restaurant and the supplier mentioned in the media, even without explicit confirmation. Additionally, the accumulation of media coverage and public discourse around the supplier’s issue can further trigger these associative processes, leading stakeholders to indirectly associate the supplier’s problem with the restaurant. As media reports about the supplier’s issue spread, even if no specific restaurant is named, the widespread nature of the coverage creates a kind of “information environment” in which stakeholders may begin to draw their own conclusions. This circumstance can be influenced by public discussions on social media, industry commentary, or news outlets that speculate about the potential impact on various businesses. Even in the absence of direct naming, the repeated exposure to the supplier’s controversy builds cognitive connections in stakeholders’ minds, prompting them to think about which businesses might be affected. Direct link In recent years, news outlets have reported on supplier malpractices affecting restaurants, ranging from food safety issues to supply malpractice. Even when restaurants are not directly responsible, their names are often included in headlines, creating the impression of complicity. For instance, Eurofood titled an article “McDonald’s supplier admits to malpractice,” while Postmedia reported 13 “KFC takes a hit in China after report said suppliers giving chickens unapproved levels of antibiotics.” Such associations can damage a restaurant’s image, erode customer trust, and negatively impact market share and brand equity (Moratis, 2016; Piotr and Dawid, 2017). Negative information also captures consumer attention more powerfully than positive, exponentially tarnishing reputations (Ahluwalia, 2000; Fombrun and Shanley, 1990). Consequently, a restaurant’s market value can be substantially affected when its name is directly linked to a supplier receiving negative media coverage. This is because consumers may associate the unfavorable news directly with the restaurant, leading to a decrease in demand for its products and services due to reduced consumer trust. Recall that consumers may associate a restaurant with the quality and integrity of its suppliers, thus, if a supplier linked to the restaurant faces bad publicity, consumers may perceive the restaurant negatively by association (Hussain et al., 2023). Along these lines, these authors also point out that as restaurants rely heavily on trust and reputation, negative news about a supplier can tarnish the restaurant's reputation, especially if consumers believe that the restaurant should have been more vigilant in selecting trustworthy suppliers. From an operational perspective, supply chain disruptions caused by supplier issues can directly impact the restaurant's ability to operate smoothly, leading to financial losses and further negative impacts on market value. Conversely, if media coverage only targets the supplier without mentioning the restaurant’s name, the impact on the restaurant’s market value may be less significant as consumers may not immediately connect the negative news to the restaurant. H2: Directly linking a restaurant to a supplier receiving bad news in the media has a greater impact on the restaurant’s market value than if the restaurant is not mentioned in the news article. 14 Differentiated effects of supplier issues The effects of supplier issues on a restaurant’s market value are nuanced, contingent upon the specific nature of the issue at hand. Acknowledging the unique characteristics of each situation, concerns related to food safety and ethical/malpractice matters such as corruption, bribery, food fraud, discrimination, and animal welfare, as well as environmental and human rights considerations, may yield varied effects on how consumers perceive and trust a restaurant’s offerings (Ryu and Lee, 2017). It entails that the influence of supplier issues on a restaurant’s market value is not solely determined by the occurrence of an issue but also by the nature and specifics of that issue. Accordingly, different categories of supplier issues can result in diverse consequences for a restaurant’s reputation and customer trust. This trust is pivotal for sustaining repeat business and positive word-of-mouth recommendations (Ji et al., 2022). The nature of the issue holds significance, given that various types of supplier issues may carry distinct implications. Therefore, the variable impact of supplier issues on a restaurant’s market value emerges from the intricate interplay between the nature of the issue and consumer perceptions of its severity, leading to varying levels of negative effects on demand and subsequent declines in market value. Contingency theory (Fiedler, 1964) and construal level theory (Liberman and Trope, 1998) help explain how different types of supplier issues might impact a restaurant’s market value differently. Applying it to supplier issues, contingency theory suggests that the impact of these issues on a restaurant’s market value varies based on the specific characteristics of the issue—such as its severity, visibility, directness of its impact on consumers, and the type of media coverage it receives. In the same vein, construal level theory posits that the psychological distance of an event or issue—whether it be temporal, spatial, social, or hypothetical—affects how people perceive, 15 interpret, and react to it. Events or issues that are perceived as psychologically close are construed more “concretely”, while those that are perceived as distant are construed more “abstractly.” In the context of food safety, environmental, and ethical issues, these are perceived as more psychologically close to consumers because they have direct, immediate, and visible impacts on their lives. Food safety directly affects consumers’ health, making it a highly sensitive issue; consequently, any reported food safety violations should lead to immediate consumer backlash, loss of trust, and a sharp decline in patronage (Yang and Baker, 2024; Yang et al., 2024). Similarly, in recent years, environmental sustainability has become a crucial factor for many consumers (Madanaguli et al., 2022). Restaurants that are seen as environmentally irresponsible may face boycotts and negative publicity, which can severely damage their reputation and market value (Kim and Stepchenkova, 2021). Ethical issues are also increasingly important to consumers (Von Walter et al., 2016). Businesses perceived as unethical face intense scrutiny and can suffer long-term reputational damage (Chen et al., 2022). Ethical malpractices, such as corruption, bribery, food fraud, discrimination, and animal welfare concerns, suggest deeper, systemic problems within the company, leading investors and customers to lose confidence. These issues are perceived as psychologically close to consumers, in line with contingency theory and construal level theory, leading to swift and strong reactions, which must be reflected in the market performance of the restaurant. Therefore, consumers are expected to react strongly and swiftly to violations in these areas (Chen et al. 2022; Kim and Stepchenkova, 2021; Madanaguli et al., 2022; Von Walter et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2024; Yang and Baker, 2024). On the other hand, human rights issues might be perceived as more psychologically distant because they are often seen as affecting people who are 16 not directly connected to the consumers' immediate experience, leading to a less intense market reaction. In line with these arguments, we propose the following hypothesis: H3: The market value of restaurants is more negatively impacted by supplier-related issues that are perceived as psychologically close to consumers (e.g., food safety, environmental sustainability, and ethical practices) compared to those perceived as psychologically distant (e.g., human rights violations). DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS To evaluate the impact of supplier issues on the performance of the restaurant firm and examine H1, we utilize an event study methodology following the guidelines outlined by McWilliams and Siegel (1997). For testing H2 and H3, we conduct regression analyses. Appendix A provides a detailed description of the methodology used. RESULTS Table 1 presents the influence of supplier issue announcements on restaurants’ performance. The findings suggest a significant negative reaction on the day prior to the supplier issue announcement, potentially attributed to information leakage reaching investors before the official news release. This result is obtained and confirmed through the parametric and non-parametric tests. Given that the sample period of 2020 and 2022 may be problematic to the restaurant industry due to the increased volatility during the COVID-19 pandemic (Lee et al., 2023), we ran the analysis without the observations corresponding to this sub-period. The results from this restricted sample are robust. Note that significant and negative effects are also found on day +3 in the whole sample, 17 but not in the restricted sample. Additionally, the cumulative abnormal returns are found significant and negative for the window (-1,0), indicating that the negative effect observed on day -1 seems to be prevalent. These findings provide empirical support for H1, suggesting that supplier issues adversely affect the market value of restaurants. The results show that the parameter associated with the direct linkage is statistically significant and positive, which does not support H2. This finding indicates that when news articles specifically mention restaurants, the negative impact on their market value is relatively lower, suggesting that a direct association between a restaurant and a supplier facing negative media attention has a less pronounced effect on the restaurant’s market value than if the restaurant were not mentioned. This outcome is unexpected, as one would assume that a direct connection between a restaurant and a 19 supplier's issue would make it easier for consumers to link the restaurant to the supplier’s problem. As further elaborated in the discussion section, we argue that the lower negative impact of direct news linkages on restaurant market value can be explained by two key reasons: i) when a restaurant is directly mentioned in negative news, it can quickly implement mitigation strategies to manage the situation and align with consumer expectations, thereby reducing the damage to its image; and ii) when a restaurant is not explicitly named, stakeholders may still associate the supplier’s issues with the restaurant, leading to negative perceptions due to a lack of direct communication or reassurance from the restaurant, resulting in a potentially more damaging “guilty by association” effect. The results also indicate that the parameter associated with human rights issues is statistically different from the parameters associated with “food safety,” “environmental issues” and the base reference “ethical issues,” thereby supporting H3. Aligned with contingency theory (Fiedler, 1964) and construal level theory (Liberman & Trope, 1998), this finding confirms that characteristics of the supplier issues, such as directness of its impact on consumers and the psychological distance affect how people perceive it. Accordingly, it seems that food safety, environmental, and ethical issues are perceived as more psychologically close to consumers because they affect them directly. None of the control variables are significant. The size of a firm, as measured by its assets, the market position, as measured by its sales, and experience, as measured by its age, do not seem to have any effects on the market value reaction to supplier malpractices. These outcomes could be because the market’s focus is more on the nature and severity of the malpractice itself rather than the firm’s size and revenue generation capabilities. Likewise, both young and old firms are equally vulnerable to negative market reactions when such issues arise. Regarding the first occurrence and cumulative occurrence of supplier malpractice, it might not significantly affect the market value, 20 potentially because a single incident might be perceived as an anomaly or because the market response is more influenced by the type and visibility of the malpractice rather than its sequence. As for the interactions “first occurrence of supplier malpractice x firm age” and “cumulative occurrences of supplier malpractice x firm age,” it seems that (1) the impact of the first malpractice incident does not vary meaningfully with the age of the firm because the market may treat first occurrences similarly regardless of how long the firm has been established; and (2) the market does not differentially penalize firms based on their age when they have multiple instances of supplier malpractices, thereby suggesting that the cumulative impact is perceived similarly across firms of different ages. From a general perspective, the non-significance of these control variables suggests that the market might prioritize the immediate and direct implications of supplier malpractices over structural firm characteristics such as size, sales, or age. CONCLUSIONS AND DISCUSSION This study aims to investigate the impact of supplier issues on the market value of restaurant firms, examining various types of supplier issues and their linkages to restaurants. Utilizing an event study methodology focusing on publicly traded restaurant firms in the United States from 2001 to 2022, the findings show a negative impact of supplier issues on restaurant market value. The study reveals that a direct linkage to a supplier issue has a lower impact than an indirect linkage, and different types of supplier issues lead to varying effects on a restaurant’s market value. 22 The finding that the direct linkage is statistically significant and positive suggests that news publications directly linked to restaurants have a comparatively lower negative effect on restaurant market value. Contrary to H2, this result implies that linking a restaurant directly to a supplier receiving negative media coverage has a less substantial effect on the restaurant’s market value than if the restaurant is not mentioned in the news article. This effect is surprising, as a direct linkage between a restaurant and a supplier’s issue would likely make it easier for consumers to associate the restaurant with the supplier’s problem. We should recall that a direct link can give rise to the perception that the restaurant is somehow accountable for the error or potentially involved in the supplier’s malpractice. Such an association has the potential to harm the restaurant’s reputation, erode customer trust, and ultimately have adverse consequences for corporate management, market share, and brand equity, aligning with Piotr and Dawid (2017) and Moratis (2016). However, two arguments can explain this finding, contrary to expectations: First, upon becoming aware of news mentioning their brand name, restaurants may promptly implement effective mitigation strategies (Seo et al., 2018; Overstreet et al., 2023). These strategies, encompassing public relations efforts, customer communication, and corrective actions, serve to minimize the damage to their image and facilitate a response to and recovery from supplier issues when their name is directly mentioned in news articles. For instance, Chipotle launched a campaign emphasizing its commitment to food safety after its 2015 E. coli outbreak, including public statements from the CEO and detailed explanations of the steps the company was taking to ensure such an event would not happen again (Cha and Cichy, 2018). Similarly, if a restaurant is associated with a supplier accused of environmental violations, it may swiftly sever ties with that supplier and publicize the change. McDonald's has taken similar actions in the past, such as when it switched to cage-free eggs and sustainable beef suppliers in response to consumer concerns 23 about animal welfare and environmental impact (Lusk, 2019). This not only mitigates immediate damage but also aligns the brand with consumer expectations. Also, a restaurant can engage proactively with the media by providing press releases that outline the steps being taken to address the issue. Even if anecdotally, KFC effectively used Twitter to manage a crisis in the UK when it ran out of chicken (Hale, 2018), humorously acknowledging the situation and keeping customers informed about when the issue would be resolved, thereby providing real-time updates on the situation and corrective measures. Second, in line with the literature, even when a restaurant is not explicitly mentioned in a news publication, stakeholders may establish indirect connections between supplier malpractices and the restaurant’s reputation. This occurs by triggering and forming associations in their memory network, as proposed by Collins and Loftus’ (1975) associative network memory paradigm. These stakeholders may associate a supplier’s issue with the restaurant itself, leading to a negative perception of the restaurant, even if it is not directly responsible for the misconduct (Jung and Lee, 2022). This “guilty by association” phenomenon can be more damaging to the restaurant’s reputation than explicit mentions, potentially due to a perceived lack of reassurance on the part of the restaurant. When a restaurant is not explicitly named in the news, there may be a perception that it is hiding or avoiding transparency, even if that is not the case. Stakeholders may expect restaurants to proactively address the issue and communicate their commitment to quality and safety, which might not occur if they are not named, resulting in a detrimental effect on the restaurant’s market value. The results also indicate that the parameter associated with human rights issues is statistically significant, differing from the parameters associated with “food safety,” “environmental issues,” and the base reference “ethical issues,” which supports H3 in line with contingency theory (Fiedler, 24 1964) and construal level theory (Liberman & Trope, 1998). The positive parameter of human rights shows that, while all four categories of supplier malpractices are damaging to firm value, “food safety,” “environmental issues,” and “ethical issues” have stronger negative effects on the market value of restaurants. Food safety directly affects consumers’ health, making it a highly sensitive issue; consequently, any reported food safety violations can lead to immediate consumer backlash, loss of trust, and a sharp decline in patronage, in line with Yang and Baker (2024) and Yang et al. (2024). The direct impact on customer health and the immediate visibility of food safety issues seem to result in strong negative market reactions. Similarly, in recent years, environmental sustainability has become a crucial factor for many consumers, as pointed out by Madanaguli et al. (2022). Restaurants that are seen as environmentally irresponsible may face boycotts and negative publicity, which can severely damage their reputation and market value, in line with Kim and Stepchenkova (2021). It is no wonder that environmental issues often garner significant media attention, leading to broader awareness and a more substantial impact on the restaurant’s market performance. As emphasized by Von Walter et al. (2016), ethical issues are also increasingly important to consumers. Businesses perceived as unethical face intense scrutiny and can suffer long-term reputational damage, as found by Chen et al. (2022). Ethical malpractices, such as corruption, bribery, food fraud, discrimination, and animal welfare concerns, suggest deeper, systemic problems within the company, leading investors and customers to lose confidence. These issues are perceived as psychologically close to consumers, leading to swift and strong reactions, which are reflected in the market performance of the restaurant. In contrast, while human rights violations are serious and damaging, the results suggest that their impact on market value is less intense. This difference may be explained by the psychological 25 distance of human rights issues from the immediate consumer experience, in line with Liberman and Trope (1998). Since human rights violations are often perceived as more distant or abstract compared to food safety, environmental, or ethical issues, they result in a relatively less intense immediate market reaction. The perceived distance from the consumer’s immediate experience may also contribute to food safety, environmental, and ethical issues receiving more intense and sustained media coverage compared to human rights issues. This media focus can amplify the negative impact on a restaurant’s market value as public reaction becomes swift and widespread. According to these results, the influence of supplier issues on a restaurant’s market value is not solely determined by the occurrence of an issue but also by the nature and specifics of that issue, thereby underscoring the contingent nature of the impact of supplier-related issues on market value, as explained by contingency theory and construal level theory. Theoretical Implications Theoretically, our findings enrich the understanding of the intricate relationship between supplier issues and restaurant performance, contributing to the existing literature on external factors’ impact on firms’ market value. The observation that indirect links exert a more significant influence on restaurant market value than direct links aligns with the associative network memory paradigm, emphasizing stakeholders’ pivotal role in forming perceptions and associations. This underscores the importance of comprehending the dynamics of memory and associations in shaping consumer behavior and judgments, suggesting that a negative impression in one realm (such as supplier misconduct) can reverberate into opinions in another area (specifically, the restaurant’s image). 26 Another critical theoretical implication of our findings underscores the necessity for a more nuanced approach to investigating the impact of supply chain issues on firm performance. The differentiation of supplier issue types, encompassing food safety, environmental, human rights, and ethical issues, along with the distinction between direct and indirect linkages between the restaurant and the supplier’s issues, enlightens the intricate interplay of factors influencing a restaurant’s market value. Additionally, our study accentuates the importance of comprehending the role of intermediaries, such as the media, in shaping the signaling process. By examining how direct and indirect linkages between restaurants and suppliers in news articles influence the market’s response to supplier issue announcements, we contribute to the expanding body of literature exploring the role of third parties in the transmission and interpretation of signals. Practical implications From a managerial perspective, our findings underscore the importance of fostering robust relationships with responsible and reliable suppliers, coupled with the continuous monitoring and evaluation of suppliers’ performance. Managers are advised to meticulously assess potential suppliers, considering not only their ability to deliver products and services but also their dedication to ethical, environmental, and human rights standards. By selecting suppliers aligned with the restaurant’s values, managers can reduce the likelihood of encountering supplier issues that could adversely impact their firms’ performance. Furthermore, the study suggests that effective crisis management and mitigation strategies employed by restaurants can significantly influence how they navigate supplier-related issues. This implies that businesses should proactively shape stakeholders’ perceptions and safeguard their reputation through strategic 27 actions, irrespective of whether a direct or indirect link exists between the restaurant and the supplier’s wrongdoing. Limitations and future research directions This study has several limitations. First, focusing on publicly traded restaurants may limit generalizability to smaller or privately held establishments. Second, the lack of measurement for crisis management and communication strategies used by restaurants to mitigate supplier issues represents another limitation. Future research could examine the effects of supplier issues on privately held restaurants or those in diverse subindustries such as fast casual or fine dining. In our scenario, we define the event date as the day when the supplier issue information was initially made public. Consequently, we conducted a keyword search in the Factiva database spanning from 2001 to 2022. This search includes major publicly traded restaurants in the US stock market, such as Restaurant Brands Intl Inc, Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc, McDonald’s Corp, Starbucks Corp, and Yum Brands Inc, along with their main suppliers such as Tyson Foods, Lopez Foods, Keystone Foods, McCain Foods, Cargill, Dairy Farmers of America, JBS USA, and General Mills. The stock market data are collected from Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP). The search incorporated keywords related to supplier issues, including “food safety,” “food hygiene,” “food sanitation,” “food security,” “foodborne illness,” “bribery,” “unethical,” “immoral,” “dishonest,” “wrong,” “improper,” “fraudulent,” “food fraud,” “discrimination,” “racism,” “bias,” “sexism,” “unfairness,” “animal welfare,” “animal rights,” “animal protection,” “inhumane,” “environmental issues,” “environmental problems,” “environmental challenges,” “ecological issues,” “green issues,” “habitat destruction issues,” “deforestation issues,” “human rights issues,” “social justice issues,” “equality issues,” and “corruption.” These keywords are selected based on a comprehensive review of relevant internet searches. The keywords are further refined through iterative searches in the Factiva database to ensure they capture the most relevant and frequently reported topics in the industry. Initially, 77 43 announcements are identified, but after filtering out those in close proximity to each other, the sample size was reduced to 56 announcements. Second, the duration of the event window should be established. To address potential information leaks or delays in investors’ responses, we employ a (-3,+3) event window to examine the potential presence of excess returns before and after the announcement. Although longer event windows may increase the likelihood of discovering a greater number of excess returns, they also carry a significant drawback: these extended windows are more susceptible to being influenced by other events unrelated to the announcements analyzed in this study. Consequently, we cannot guarantee that any potential excess returns discovered far from the event day genuinely derive from the given announcement or some other external news (McWilliams and Siegel, 1997). Therefore, a (-3,+3) window appears to strike an ideal balance, being long enough to capture information pre- and post- announcement but not too long to be affected by confounding effects. Third, any potential confounding effects should be identified. To prevent spurious abnormal returns, it is essential to detect and remove events unrelated to the supplier’s issue announcements that may occur during the event window. To achieve this, we employ the Factiva database to search for news items not connected to the supplier’s issues but that may emerge in the (+3,-3) window. As a consequence, the final sample is 50 announcements. Following this, the collected data points are organized into distinct groups. These categories encompass “direct link”, where the restaurant’s name is explicitly associated with the supplier’s issues in news articles, and “indirect link”, where the restaurant’s name is not explicitly connected to the supplier’s issues in news articles. The identification and categorization of direct and indirect links is conducted through a detailed analysis of each announcement. This involves reviewing the content of news articles and press releases for explicit mentions of the restaurant names in 44 connection with the supplier issues, thereby classifying them as direct links. Announcements that involve the suppliers but do not explicitly mention the restaurant names are categorized as indirect links. This method ensures that the links are classified based on the visibility and directness of the association between the restaurant and the supplier issue, allowing for an accurate measurement of the impact of public perception on stock performance. Furthermore, the collected data points are subdivided into various issue types to explore the diverse impacts of different categories of issues, such as “food safety issues (25 cases),” “environmental issues (8),” “human rights issues (8),” and “ethical issues (9).” The latter is used as the reference category in the regression model to avoid perfect collinearity. This categorization of issues is strategically aligned with the aim to assess the multifaceted impact of supplier problems on restaurant firms. The four categories are chosen because the data points collected fall under them. Even if it is an ad hoc classification, by categorizing the issues, we can distinctly measure the differential impacts of various types of supplier problems, providing a nuanced analysis of how different issues influence restaurant performance differently. In this analysis, the abnormal returns linked to each announcement serve as the dependent variable. The independent variables include both direct and indirect connections (with the indirect link as the reference point for model estimation) and the categories of supplier issues identified, namely food safety issues, environmental concerns, human rights and ethical issues (with ethical issues serving as the baseline reference). Apart from these main variables, several control variables are included: i) Assets. Firms with larger assets are generally considered more stable and capable of weathering adverse events, and they may have more resources to manage crises, mitigate risks, and recover from setbacks (Ivanov, 2016); ii) Sales. Sales figures indicate revenue generation capabilities, with high numbers reflecting a strong market position and competitive advantage (Elliot and Elliot, 2019), which can reassure investors about the firm’s future prospects; iii) Firm age. Older firms are likely to have experience and long-standing relationships with stakeholders, which can buffer against negative impacts from supplier malpractices (Brawn & Šević, 2018); iv) First occurrence of supplier malpractice. The first occurrence of supplier malpractice can have a significant impact because it represents a new and unexpected risk to investors. The market might react strongly to the initial news, in line with Bernard and Nicolau (2022). The first instance can severely damage the 48 restaurant’s reputation, particularly if the firm is perceived as having inadequate due diligence processes. Consequently, the initial occurrence can lead to a reassessment of the firm’s risk profile by investors, who might respond by selling off shares, thereby lowering the market value; v) Cumulative occurrences of supplier malpractice. Multiple instances of an event may have different effects on stock market returns (Bernard & Nicolau, 2022). Specifically, supplier malpractice can reinforce the perception that the firm has systemic issues with its supply chain management and quality control. Repeated malpractices can erode trust among consumers, investors, and other stakeholders. This erosion can lead to declines in market value as the cumulative impact builds. Additionally, interacting “first occurrence of supplier malpractice” and “cumulative occurrences of supplier malpractice” with firm age can provide insights into how the experience of the firm modifies the impact of these malpractices on market value: vi) regarding the interaction “first occurrence of supplier malpractice x firm age,” given that older firms typically have a more established reputation, the first occurrence of supplier malpractice might have a more significant negative impact on older firms because stakeholders might have higher expectations for established firms to have robust supply chain management. event date, the reaction does not necessarily have to happen on the event date; it may happen prior to the event date or after the event date. That is the reason why event studies are, by definition, designed to use event windows to identify the day investors incorporate the information, thereby detecting the day the impact on stock prices happens. In fact, it is standard in event studies to analyze stock reactions not only on the day of the event itself, but also in a small number of days in a window enveloping the chosen event day (McWilliams and Siegel; 1997; Sorescu et al., 2017. The inclusion of days prior to the event date allows for the possibility that news regarding the event could have leaked prior to the official announcement. When information regarding an event may have leaked to investors prior to the official announcement, investors would update their expectations about the firm’s performance outlook at that earlier stage. Such leakages are, in fact, quite common in the literature. See for example, Kyle et al. (1992) who found reactions on window (-2,0), Byrd et al. (1998) on window (-3,0), Koh and Lee (2013) on day -2, Homburg et al. (2014) on window (-1,0), Nicolau and Sharma (2019) on day -1, or Kim and Tang (2020) on days -5 and -4. In other words, while the event date serves as the reference point, in event studies, we do not know when the reaction occurs exactly until the abnormal returns are observed. The date the information is "officially" released (the event date) may differ from when investors actually become aware of it. The strength of event studies lies in their ability to capture the market’s reaction to new information as it becomes available. Following McWilliams and Siegel (1997) and Gielens et al. (2018), once the day or days exhibiting a significant reaction are identified, this day (or days) will be used. In our study, day -1 is the only 55 day that shows significant abnormal returns across all tests employed and across both the entire sample and the Covid-19-controlled reduced sample. The other days of the windows do not show values statistically and significantly different from zero, so there is no cross-sectional variation in the abnormal returns across firms. JSON: Name: supplier_malpractice_event_study Title: Event-study and panel-regression analysis of the effect of media-reported supplier malpractices on publicly traded restaurant firms' market value Short Hypothesis: Media reports of supplier malpractices cause statistically significant negative abnormal stock returns for associated publicly traded restaurant firms within a (-3,+3) trading-day event window. Related Work: Existing research applies event-study methods and accounting/marketing analyses to quantify firm value effects from adverse incidents, corporate social responsibility signals, and food-safety crises. Prior event-study approaches primarily use market- or multi-factor return models and standard parametric tests; some extend to nonparametric and variance-robust methods. Studies on supplier or supply-chain incidents typically focus on single incident types (e.g., food safety) or aggregate retail/wholesale categories rather than isolating restaurants. Literature using signaling theory highlights how third-party news acts as market signals, but empirical work rarely separates news that directly names the focal firm from news that leaves linkage implicit. Limitations in prior approaches include limited disaggregation of malpractice types, insufficient control for pre-announcement information leaks, sparse use of multi-factor or heteroskedasticity-aware return models, small or non-representative samples (e.g., private firms excluded), and inadequate robustness checks for media-driven classification and temporal confounds such as pandemic-related volatility. Abstract: This study quantifies how media-reported supplier malpractices affect the market value of publicly traded restaurant firms. We combine an event-study framework with cross-sectional regression analysis to measure abnormal returns around supplier-issue announcements and to test how linkage visibility (directly naming restaurants versus indirect reporting) and malpractice category (food safety, ethical, environmental, human rights) mediate market responses. The research contributes (1) a systematic classification of supplier-issue linkages in news; (2) abnormal-return estimation using multi-factor return models with heteroskedasticity controls; and (3) a panel regression that isolates linkage and issue-type effects while controlling for firm characteristics and repeated incidents. Expected outcomes are statistically significant negative abnormal returns associated with supplier malpractices, heterogeneous effects across issue types, and a differential impact depending on whether media explicitly name the restaurant. Results will clarify how third-party supplier events transmit reputational and financial risk to downstream firms and inform empirical signaling and associative-memory explanations for market reactions. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Stock returns and firm fundamentals: CRSP and Compustat for all US publicly traded restaurant firms, 2001–2022. (2) News corpus: Factiva full-text search for supplier malpractice events and firm mentions; manual validation of event text to classify linkage (direct vs indirect) and issue type (food safety, ethical, environmental, human rights). (3) Factor returns: Fama-French three factors + momentum (Carhart) from Kenneth French data library; S&P500 and Dow for robustness. Sample construction: Identify unique news events; remove overlapping/confounding corporate events in ±3 trading days; final N ≈ 50 events (report exact N in reproducible code). Event-study setup: Estimation window = 255 trading days ending 5 days before event; event windows = [-3,+3], primary dependent ARs evaluated per day; compute abnormal returns using four-factor model coefficients estimated on the estimation window. Volatility control: estimate GARCH(1,1) conditional variances for robustness and use standardized abnormal returns. Statistical tests: Brown-Warner parametric t-tests and Giaccotto-Sfiridis jackknife nonparametric tests for AR and CAR significance. Regression analysis: Dependent variable = AR(-1) (also run AR(0) and CAR(-1,0) as sensitivity). Independent variables = direct_link dummy (1 if firm named), issue_type dummies (reference: ethical), controls = log(assets), log(sales), firm_age, first_occurrence dummy, cumulative_occurrences, interactions (first_occurrence×firm_age, cumulative_occurrences×firm_age). Fixed effects: firm and year dummies. Standard errors clustered at firm level. Baselines: (A) market-model (single-factor), (B) Fama-French three-factor, (C) four-factor (primary), (D) four-factor + GARCH standardization. Ablation studies: (1) remove direct/indirect classification to measure pooled effect; (2) exclude control variables; (3) alternate event windows [-1,+1], [-5,+5]; (4) alternative dependent AR days (AR(-2), AR(0)); (5) restrict sample by excluding 2020–2022. Evaluation metrics: mean AR and CAR values, t-statistics and p-values for event tests, regression coefficients with standard errors, adjusted R-squared, effect sizes (percentage point change in mean returns), and robustness indicators (sign-change across baselines). Report multiple-testing adjusted p-values (Bonferroni and FDR). Risk Factors and Limitations: News-linkage misclassification risk from ambiguous articles and incomplete supplier–restaurant disclosure; measurement error in linking suppliers to restaurants leading to attenuation bias. Small sample size of validated events reduces statistical power and increases Type II error risk; sample restricted to publicly traded firms limits external validity for private/smaller restaurants. Pre-announcement information leakage and confounding simultaneous events introduce endogeneity and limit causal interpretation. Market volatility heteroskedasticity (notably during COVID-19) can bias standard tests if not fully modeled. Omitted variable bias from unobserved firm-specific crisis-management actions or concurrent reputation shocks. Media selection bias: high-profile firms are overrepresented in news, skewing effect estimates. Multiple hypothesis testing increases false-positive risk if not corrected. Model specification risks: factor-model misspecification, incorrect event-window choice, and clustering/serial correlation not fully accounted for can distort inference. Results may not generalize across countries, non-stock-market firms, or non-restaurant sectors.
